newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU voices need for EMU policy coordination.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU voices need for EMU policy coordination.

text.p: European Union finance ministers, determined to project a united front on the planned single currency, emphasised on Monday the need for greater economic policy coordination after EMU begins in 1999.
Europe's disturbingly high unemployment rate was the focus of attention for all ministers in their opening remarks of the first ministerial gathering under the Luxembourg EU presidency.

Led in particular by France, which has put the jobs issue at the top of the European agenda, there appeared to be broad acceptance that economic policy must be better coordinated after the euro is launched on January 1, 1999.

"We all know good economic policy is one that pays heed to all the elements of the policy mix," said French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn, adding that France remained firmly committed to the single currency.
"We are very much closer to the finishing line now. We simply need to persevere," he added.
The new French government has said it will not strictly meet the deficit criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU) this year, but that the single currency will go ahead on time anyway.

This has posed a problem for Germany, which is under intense domestic pressure not to allow a weak euro be be created. Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber said in a newspaper interview on Monday that a delay in the euro was preferable to a weak one.

Outlining Luxembourg's work programme for the next six months, Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker stressed the need to bolster employment through constructive policies which avoided raising false hopes.
"We must be wary of creating expectations we are unable to fulfil," Juncker told his colleagues.
"Nonetheless we must not be shy of ambition."
Differences over how best to create employment have long dominated EU talks, with many countries believing that the problem can only be resolved at the national level.
"The fundamental aim of free markets must be maintained," said German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, adding that the EU needed to find a way to address the issue of "efficient" policy coordination.
One of the primary worries for EMU in the aftermath of the new French government's electoral victory is a split between Bonn and Paris over how economic policy should be managed under monetary union.
France has put forward a series of proposals aimed to redress the balance of power away from a European Central Bank and more towards national governments.
Worried that too much importance has been attached to German model of monetary stability, the French government has managed to shift the debate towards economic growth and employment.
The key concern for Germany is avoiding a scenario which politicises the policy decisions of an independent central bank.
The ministers also urged more rapid progress towards tax harmonisation within the EU, with many citing the harm done by tax competition between countries.
Separately, the ministers approved Italy's plans for qualifying for the single currency.
"The Italian convergence programme very clearly shows that Italy is moving in a good direction," Luxembourg's Juncker told reporters as he arrived for the meeting.
But Juncker, who is both finance minister and prime minister of the Grand Duchy, said Rome needed to do more to get its economy in line with others.
"We have to encourage them to take further steps," he said.

Italy's hopes of joining the single currency in 1999, once considered slim, have been bolstered recently by growing expectations that the entry criteria for the euro will be applied in a flexible manner.

The Italian blueprint to be studied by the ministers foresees a budget deficit of 3.0 percent of Gross Domestic Product this year, in line with the criterion for EMU. It predicts the ratio will drop to 2.8 percent in 1998.
The ministers are expected, however, to tell Italy that it needs to do more to curb spending, particularly on pensions, if it is to reach these goals.
